The following note states Maintenance is required to verify sidestick transducers associated with ELACs (Elevator and Aileron Computer) and operative SECs are operative. This sentence seems redundant to what the flight crew are asked to do in the procedure, which appears to ask the crew to pressurize all 3 hydraulic systems and do a flight control check for each operative ELAC and SEC. I say appears because this was far from clear in my conversation with the Airframe Technician. In fact, the verbiage appears different from the FMâ€™s description of the flight control check, which states both engines and generators must be running. So why am I doing this at the gate using the blue system on the aft overhead maintenance panel? At this point I am making educated guesses. The system training we as aircrew are given does not support doing this type of deferral. Having been through 4 full-course for the bus, the switch was identified as being for Maintenance use only. If I need to be able to do this type of deferral, I need better and more thorough system knowledge of what I am doing and why I am doing it, either from the Airframe Technician or ground school. I would propose a Pepsi blind taste test - call 3 different airframe technicians and ask them to explain this deferral. My bet is you would get 3 completely different answers. I just donâ€™t think our system ground training program supports this type of deferral. For a deferral of this type there needs to be a one paragraph-big picture of what you as the pilot are trying to accomplish. Pilot-to-pilot. If the Airframe Technician canâ€™t explain it to me adequately, and neither myself or the FO (First Officer) understands what is being conveyed, then we as a crew cannot meet the FOM requirements to have a complete understanding of the maintenance status. This leads to the philosophical debate of how much information needs to be taught in ground school, but I would submit for deferrals such as this we need much more. In addition, this day we received an email from ZZZ1 Operations stating there was a large weather system moving through, with the likelihood of diverts. Taking an aircraft that required maintenance action every leg to an alternate could be problematic.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported confusion over whether certain components of the flight control system were deferrable and ultimately refused the aircraft.

2.Make Model Name: Cessna Aircraft Undifferentiated or Other Model

1.Text: I was training on LCL. There was a line of thunderstorms to east with moderate to extreme precipitation. Runways XXR/XXC/XXL in use. Aircraft X was on an ILS Runway XXR approaching ZZZZZ the final approach fix when he checked on the frequency. I issued traffic to Aircraft X at his two o'clock and 2nm, same altitude moving south toward him type unknown suggest you descend. I then called ZZZ sector and asked him if he was talking to the unidentified aircraft in the Class C and he said negative. I went back to Aircraft X and updated him on the traffic at his one o'clock and 1nm southbound type unknown and Aircraft X reported him in sight. Aircraft X went underneath the unidentified aircraft by about 400 ft. and landed without incident. I asked Aircraft X on arrival what type aircraft it was and he stated some sort of Cessna. Traffic [should be] issued sooner to Aircraft X via the approach sector.

Synopsis.Narrative: TRACON Controller reported an NMAC occurred between a large transport on final approach and small aircraft which was not in communication with ATC.

1.Text: During taxi-out for Aircraft X, [the] Flight Attendant (FA) injured her left elbow by falling against a quarter-turn in the aft galley as a result of my Captain having to suddenly stop the aircraft in order to prevent a possible left wingtip collision with an aircraft on an adjacent taxiway. During taxi out of ZZZ, we were taxiing eastbound on Taxiway XX. We were instructed by ZZZ Ground Control to yield to an aircraft that was joining Taxiway XX on Taxiway XY coming from an eastbound taxi on Taxiway XZ. There was a Company Aircraft Y that was in front of us, joining Taxiway XY from Taxiway XZ at the conjunction of taxiways XX, XZ, and XY. I assumed that the Company Aircraft Y was the aircraft we were to hold for, as ZZZ Ground did not specify an aircraft type, e.g., 787 or Airbus. Aircraft Y was far enough ahead and was not a conflict, so I continued to taxi on Taxiway XX towards Runway XXR, as our instructions were to taxi to XXR using taxiways XX and XX1. As we moved towards the conjunction of taxiways XX, XZ, and XY, I noticed an, up to this point, unseen Company Aircraft Z coming on Taxiway XZ from behind and to our left at a good pace, over my left shoulder view from the cockpit. I did not realize or expect that it was the aircraft that ZZZ Ground had instructed us to hold for, so I continued taxiing on Taxiway XX. Over the next few seconds, as we approached the conjunction of Taxiway XX and XY, I noticed the Company Aircraft Z on Taxiway XZ had caught up and was parallel with our aircraft, an A320, and was continuing towards Taxiway XY in order to join Taxiway XX in front of our aircraft. During this time, I instructed my FO (First Officer) to start the number 2 engine in order to be prepared for takeoff once reaching the runway. As such, he was heads down and did not notice the taxi conflict with the other Aircraft Z. Both aircraft were nearly at Taxiway XY when ZZZ Ground noticed the conflict and informed us that the Company Aircraft Z on our left was the actual aircraft we were supposed to yield for, vs. the earlier Aircraft Y. I noticed the Company Aircraft Z had initiated a turn towards Taxiway XY and as such, I ended up using firm braking in order to stop our aircraft in order to prevent any possible left wingtip conflict/contact, and in order to comply with ZZZ Ground instructions to hold short of Taxiway XY in order to yield to the other aircraft. During the braking maneuver, [a] FA (Flight Attendant) was facing towards the aft of the aircraft and lost her footing in the aft galley. She then fell backwards, towards the front of the aircraft, striking her left elbow on a quarter turn in the aft galley cart stowage area. Her impact with the quarter turn was hard enough to cause a painful injury to her elbow. I contacted the Purser and asked if the flight attendants were OK. I was informed that [the] FA was injured, and the nature of her injury was serious enough that we needed to return to the gate and to have medical personnel meet the aircraft. We coordinated with ZZZ Operations and returned to Gate XX, our original departure gate. We had paramedics, a Flight Operations Representative, and eventually an Flight Attendant Representative meet us. The paramedics tended to [the] FA and she was taken off the aircraft in their care. During the process, they had arranged for a replacement FA to work the flight segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I discussed the overall situation with [the] ZZZ Flight Operations Representative. I called the Chief Pilot and left a message with brief details of the incident. My First Officer and I made the determination that we were fit to fly the segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After further consult with [the] Flight Operations Representative and taking care of all necessary actions, we continued with the flight.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported a Flight Attendant falling and getting injured during an abrupt braking to avoid a wingtip collision with another aircraft during taxi-out.

1.Text: At FL390, pressurization in cabin started to increase. Started a descent and went through the checklist. Shortly afterwards the cabin went to 15,000 feet and O2 masks were deployed. Had requested priority handling with Dispatch and ATC. Alerted FAs (Flight Attendant) of the problem, what to expect. Landed in ZZZ1, intended destination. Debriefed crew, Maintenance, Dispatch, [and] union. Everyone said it was done by textbook procedures.

2.Text: AT FL390 we were cleared to descend and passing through FL360 we noticed the cabin altitude increasing. We told ATC and initiated an immediate descent. Complied with ECAMs and QRH procedures. Briefed FAs (Flight Attendant) and safely landed aircraft. Debriefed with crew, Maintenance, Dispatch, passengers, and emergency medical support staff.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported loss of cabin pressure control and requested priority handling and proceeded to land at destination airport.

1.Text: Crew departed late due to brake accumulator issues on previous aircraft, and a potential one on this aircraft. Ground Ops were completely normal and the FO (First Officer) had no problems deploying the flaps to 3 for takeoff. Takeoff was normal and as we were turning to an assigned heading, we reached the cleanup altitude. I called for flaps 1 and noticed that the FO had some what I felt was minor difficulty bringing the flaps up to 1. This is not unusual, a hand slips, or the lever used to move the flap handle out of the detects isn't gripped correctly for easy retraction. I thought little of it. When I called for flaps UP, the raising was again delayed, and I noticed my FO reaching around with his right hand to put both hands on the flap lever to get it up. We talked about him having trouble getting them up, and I flew the aircraft only to ensure that I did not over speed the flaps. Eventually he was able to get them up which I saw on the speed tape on the PFD and I verified on the display, and flap handle position. We discussed what had happened a bit but decided to focus on safely exiting the terminal area and getting to altitude since the aircraft was now in the safe, and proper configuration. We made a plan to contact Maintenance Control at cruise and notify them of the problem and get advice about continuing the flight. After reaching altitude, the FO told me what he had encountered and explained how difficult it was to move the lever that released the flap handle from the detent to raise the flaps. A phone patch was initiated with dispatch and Maintenance Control and we discovered that our radio 2 wasn't able to receive over long distances. We ended up substituting radio 3 for radio 2 and temporarily disabling ACARS to complete the phone patch. Maintenance Control was very helpful on the phone patch and felt like he knew what the problem was. Maintenance Control was asked if he felt the aircraft should continue to ZZZZ, and he wanted it to go to a maintenance hub. As a Captain, I agreed with that thought process and asked the Dispatcher to bring in the Ops Manager so that we could all agree on a plan of action. We could have landed the aircraft at ZZZZ if there had been a flap malfunction, but the aircraft would have been stuck there quite a while. Eventually after consideration of landing lengths, the close to overweight landing weight of the aircraft, and the potential for wet runways in ZZZ1, that the best and safest place to divert the aircraft would be ZZZ1 in case the flaps would not deploy normally. Consideration was based on the worst case, flaps up scenario. Destination was changed with ATC once the plan was agreed upon by all parties and the phone patch was terminated and ACARS restored. Maintenance Control was asked via ACARS if we should leave the flaps down after landing and they asked them to retract them as much as we could. Fortunately, the landing in ZZZ1 was uneventful. The flaps deployed normally. Upon taxi-in. The flaps were retraced to position 1, where the handle binding began to be very difficult to overcome. Upon arrival at the gate, after shutdown, I tried to move the lever that releases the flap handle from the detent and found that it was impossible to move with just one hand.

2.Text: We were doing a flaps 3 takeoff from [Runway] XXL. After the acceleration altitude, and above flap retraction speed, the pilot flying called for flaps to 1. I noticed, while moving the lever from 3 to 1, that the flap lever was nowhere near as smooth and free moving as it usually is, rather, it was quite difficult to move. As we accelerated through flap 1 retraction speed, it took considerable effort to get the lever out of the detent. I mentioned it to the captain who quickly made sure to raise the nose and not over speed the flaps as I used both hands to get the flap lever compressed and moved to the up position. The flaps moved as expected, with no issues, the flight control page showed normal, and the hydraulic page showed normal. We continued the climb out of ZZZ, and when reaching a safe altitude, I took the controls and radios with ATC, while the captain initiated an incredibly detailed conversation with dispatch and Maintenance Control. After exhausting every bit of information we could give, and every insight Maintenance Control had, the decision was made with dispatch and everyone in planning that they were talking to, to divert to ZZZ1 instead of potentially having a flight control issue on landing in ZZZZ, on a shorter runway, at an international station, and then leaving the plane there. We didn't [request priority] but asked approach to slow down early to get the flaps out and make sure they extended. We had planned every contingency for having to go around and then [request priority] if they didn't, and were ready to run whichever QRH abnormal procedure would have applied based on where the flaps ended up. On the approach, the flaps came down just fine and a normal landing was made. After landing, we planned, with maintenance approval, to attempt to retract the flaps but to stop if they locked again and not force anything. The lever was much less stiff from flaps full to flaps 1 than earlier, but again locked at the detent there. We left the flaps at 1 into the gate, let ramp know to tell anyone they could, and had maintenance meet us there. Sounded like they were going to replace the entire flap lever section.

Synopsis.Narrative: Flight crew reported difficulty in raising the trailing edge flaps and elected to divert instead of risking a grounded aircraft at an outstation.

1.Text: This event occurred during preflight at the gate. The aircraft arrived at ZZZ gate XX from the maintenance hanger eight minutes before boarding time. After review of the AML, I confirmed the aircraft had a couple of MEL items including a #2 engine thrust reverser inoperative. We contacted maintenance for three additional items, including excessively high wheel brake temperatures on wheels three and four. Those temperatures were 340 degrees C and 270 degrees C, respectively. When the mechanic arrived at the aircraft, I asked him for the reason the brakes were so hot after a tow or taxi delivery from the hanger. He inspected the brakes and found them to be "very warm." He also ran a few diagnostic tests. Unfortunately the mechanic could not give an adequate explanation for the high wheel brake temperatures, nor could he verify the proper functioning of the wheel brakes on the right main gear. I refused the aircraft on the basis of safety-of-flight because I felt the aircraft was unsafe to operate with an unknown wheel brake issue coupled with an inoperative thrust reverser. The primary causal factor for refusing the aircraft was the unknown reason for the hot brakes. This issue was not resolved to my satisfaction. The risk of operating the aircraft with both a brake issue and inoperative reverser was too high to warrant continuation of the flight. Maintenance personnel should resolve obvious aircraft issues before releasing the aircraft to the flight crew.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported refusing the aircraft due to a deferred thrust reverser and high brake temperatures that maintenance could not explain.

1.Text: When we arrived in ZZZ to start our trip we meet with the inbound crew to discuss the inbound leg and aircraft. There was no mention from them about any odors or problems with the aircraft. When we boarded the aircraft we were over come by a strong smell throughout the plane. Looking back it was strange the previous crew didn't mention this. It was similar to a strong carpet cleaner smell or an odor like when you clean an oven. There was no indication of fire or smoke much less any indications of a malfunction. We discussed the issue with the crew and found no reasons not to continue safely. As we boarded the aircraft several passengers started to complain especially in the rear cabin about the odor. We discussed what the cause of the smell could be and determined that it was not a safety of flight issue since we could not isolate any problems. All systems operated normally. We agreed to continue on the short flight to ZZZ1 hoping that at altitude the fresh air would dispute any smell. We felt that since there was smoke all around the area from west coast wild fires that could possibly be the cause. At cruise the smell seemed to disappear in the cockpit but as we got closer to our destination the FA'S informed us that it remained in the cabin. There was no smoke or any indications of a malfunction. They then stated that many passengers complained that they were starting to get headaches and feel bad. We asked if there any immediate concerns and were informed there were none. Inbound we decided to inform maintenance control that there was an odor which seemed to be coming from the gasper vents via an MRM entry so that on arrival they could trouble shoot and see if they could remove it. After landing we started the APU and received a low oil level indication. Not sure if this contributed to the problem or not as we accepted the aircraft in ZZZ with the APU operating and had no indications of any problems at that time. Arriving at the gate we noticed that the smell in the cockpit remained but the cabin was stronger. We had an hour on the ground before our next flight so felt that the problem could be resolved. After block in we meet with maintenance and he noticed the smell as well. His feeling is it smelled like burning oil. We had no indications at any time of an overheat or fire on any system. I then received a call from Name our Chief Pilot to contact Name 1 in Maintenance Control for some questions. I was asked generic questions about the entire flight to help trouble shoot the problem. As I stated everything went great expect for the strong smell. They removed the aircraft from service and we continued our trip with another aircraft. The entire crew handled the situation professionally and with merit. I applaud how we worked together to assist passengers needs and answer any questions or concerns they may have had. The flight was concluded safely and professional with our [company] principles.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported a fumes event of varying intensity from preflight to arrival at destination where maintenance removed the aircraft from service.

1.Text: Flight planning, preflight, ground operations, and takeoff were accomplished per SOP and were uneventful. Captain was pilot flying. Passing 18000 STD, altimeter was selected and AP 1 was selected. At XA:17, we got a master caution light, with HYD G RSVR LO LVL, HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR, and HYD G SYS LO PR displayed on the upper ECAM. After confirming no Green Hydraulic QTY, I asked the FO (First Officer) to request to stop climb and return to field. Captain continued to fly and handle radios. FO accomplished the ECAM procedures, turning off the PTU and Green Eng 1 Pump. QRH was referenced after ECAMs completed, screens normal. We requested priority handling with ATC. Advised Dispatch through ACARS that we had lost all Green Hydraulic QTY, were returning to ZZZ, and would require a tow off runway due to loss of nosewheel steering. Purser was advised of the malfunction, that we were returning to field in 20 minutes, and a cabin prep was not required. A visual approach to XXL was briefed after runway assignment and the descent checklist was accomplished. Aircraft was configured early due to slow flaps/slats and alternate gravity gear extension. Approach and landing were accomplished per SOP and were uneventful. Aircraft was stopped straight ahead on centerline. Engines shut down with timing after starting APU. Aircraft was inspected by Fire Response Team, confirming gear doors down and fluid [was] leaking from under plane behind gear. Super tug arrived and towed us clear of runway to Gate XXX.

2.Text: On climbout passing approximately 21,000 feet, we got an ECAM indicating loss of the green system, LO G Press, and another green system ECAM but I cannot recall it now. We ran the ECAM action items which had us turn off the PTU and Eng 1 G pump. As soon as the ECAM action items were complete, we communicated with ATC, advising them we needed to stop our climb, and requested priority handling and requested a return to ZZZ. The CA (Captain) and I split up the flying and comm duties, he advised the FA's (Flight Attendant) of our situation, and sent a message to Dispatch. I talked to ATC and flew the aircraft for a brief time while he handled the message to Dispatch. We got the expanded checklist and discussed the effects of [a] loss of the green system in terms of manual cranking of the gear and needing to stop on the runway due to loss of steering, which the CA sent an ACARs to the station to start working on a tow for us to minimize us sitting on the runway. I also advised ATC to let ZZZ know we would be a full-stop on the runway and would need to be towed. We were given priority handling back to ZZZ and we briefed the approach and threats of a go-around since the gear could not be retracted once it was hand-cranked down. The CA flew the approach XXL and the landing and stopping at the end of the runway was uneventful. We dropped the landing gear pins to the tug team and got towed back to the gate. We debriefed once we were off the aircraft and the passengers disembarked. The CA was cool, calm, and collected and flew a textbook approach. We worked well together as a team; I can't think of much that we could have done to improve on how the situation was handled.

Synopsis.Narrative: First Officer reported loss of all green hydraulic system fluid caused an Air Turn Back and precautionary landing.

1.Text: On the final phase of the Visual Approach, backed up by the ILS Runway XY to ZZZ, with the intention to capture the glide path from above, the Auto Pilot (AP) and Auto Throttles were disengaged. Prevailing conditions were Good Visibility and varying Tail Winds of up to nine (9) Knots. During the final portion of the descent to touchdown, with a visual transition to the PAPI reference already established (PAPI were showing 3 RED-1 WHITE), the Aircraft descended below the referenced visual glide path, with the tendency to fly over the Runway XY overrun area at an altitude (AGL) of less than 50 ft. The moment the Captain, having the Pilot Monitoring (PM) duties, mentioned his estimation for being low on the glide path, the aircraft was overflying a point short of the RWY by about 500 feet. He consecutively called for a Go Around, which was immediately executed by the PF (Pilot Flying). The Flight landed after a RADAR pattern on the same runway uneventfully. [The cause was] Human Factors / Pilot Flying error on visually estimating the projected Glide Slope to Runway XY, with the current Tail Wind conditions. Root cause is the initially higher angle of descent / rate of descent to capture the glide slope from above, that ended up to an over correction - reverse situation of flying finally lower than the projected/correct slope. [I suggest] earlier Aircraft configuration for the Final Approach Phase and timely request from the ATC for lower altitudes / earlier descent to the recommended altitudes that lead to a better projected sequence of flying tasks.

2.Text: FO was flying pilot. Performed visual approach and FO had a hard time trying to catch the glide slope from above because he was trying to slow down and put flaps down while on OPEN DESC. FO called for "the bird", which caught me off guard because it is the first time anyone has asked for the flight path vector while trying to intercept the ILS and while disconnecting the AP. He not only disconnected AP but also eventually the auto thrust without previously briefing it. I told him to never disconnect the auto thrust again while trying to save a visual approach. Finally he was established on the ILS. Below 500 feet he said he was going to follow the PAPI. I glanced down at the VSI to make sure we were stable and when I looked backed up we had 4 red on the PAPIs and at the same time we received a GS GPWS warning. Became unstable. I loudly and sternly called "unstable, go-around." Performed go-around as RA called 50 feet. FO performed a soft go-around. I overrode his decision after he brought back TL (Thrust Lever) to CLB and I pushed TL to TOGA since we were in ZZZ (high airport elevation) with high OAT. I honestly could not tell you the altitude when the FO brought back the TL to CLB. I wanted to make sure we were safe since the go-around was performed at 50 feet from an unsafe position. At 50 feet RA, aircraft was not anywhere near the approach end of the runway. Came back for an uneventful landing. FO descended below glide slope and PAPI showed 4 red. Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration. Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.

Synopsis.Narrative: Flight crew reported that the First Officer made errors during final approach to landing and the Captain elected to call for a go around.

1.Text: We commenced our takeoff normally. At around 95 kts, we got an ECAM for Y RSVR Lo Lvl and Y RSVR Lo Air Pr. The Captain initiated the abort with a max speed of approximately 100 kts. All callouts and notifications were made and we were able to taxi clear of the runway and stop. ATC notified us that we had trailed smoke so we asked him to roll the ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting) equipment. We ran the rejected takeoff checklist and then ran the ECAMs of which there were several all relating to the hydraulic issue. ARFF indicated that we had dumped a lot of hydraulic fluid. We were towed to the gate for repairs and offloaded the passengers and bags.

2.Text: Received a Master Caution light and ECAM during takeoff roll on Runway XXR at ZZZ and accomplished a rejected takeoff. The Master Caution and ECAM occurred at approximately 95 kts and Reject initiated between 95-105 kts. During the reject, several ECAMS displayed indicating loss of the Yellow Hydraulic system reservoir and Yellow system air pressure. At slow speed and with normal brakes and nosewheel steering available, I opted to take high speed Taxiway XX to safely clear the runway and bring aircraft to a full stop while the First Officer coordinated with Tower controller to roll the AARF (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting) equipment as Tower stated they saw what appeared to be smoke trailing from the number two engine. While awaiting AARF response, we ran the Rejected Takeoff QRC and handled the ECAMS, started the APU and communicated with the passengers [and] inflight crew. After AARF arrival and initial inspection, we shutdown the number 2 engine with AARF on scene, then chocked the gear and shutdown the number 1 engine which had been used to keep normal brakes available. We coordinated with Operations and Ground Control for uneventful tow back to the gate for repair.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Flight Crew reported a Rejected Take Off when the Yellow Hydraulic system showed low quantity and had to be towed back to the gate.

1.Text: Dirty sock odor descending into ZZZ. [Suggest] aircraft filtered bleed air.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air Carrier Captain reported a fume event of "dirty socks odor" during descent to destination.

1.Text: Inadvertent switching off of IR1 mode selector which deactivated that associated ADIRU. ADR and IR data not available. This occurred during flight one of day two of an initial Captain upgrade. The trainee came off the B777. He has been with our company for many years. The three legs of day one was extraordinarily busy. It was immediately clear to me during those three legs he had studied hard during training and had mastered much of the material. On the first two legs of day one I had a LCA (Line Check Airman) in-training watching me conduct the line check as part of that LCA's upgrade training. I commented to the new LCA not all trainees will be so well prepared as this one. This flight was leg four of the IOE and the first flight of day two. Our transportation to the airport was 15 minutes late and there was a detour so we arrived at the aircraft about 30 minutes prior to departure. Normally, I introduce myself to all the FAs (Flight Attendant). However, because we were on IOE, [we] were somewhat late to the aircraft and on Release 6. I only introduced myself to the FM. I felt I did not have time go to the back to introduce myself to the FAs assigned to the rear of the aircraft. We had been in the seat for approximately 3 hours. The upgrade Captain requested I ask the FM to prepare the meals and that we would then take a restroom break when the meals were ready. I did so. The FM called us about 25 minutes later to state the meals were ready. The upgrade Captain offered me the opportunity to use the Lav first. I declined and said he should go first and I would then go. The door chime rang and then I heard a knock. That knock is not standard. However, it occurs occasionally with legacy Company 2 flight attendants. We put on our masks. I saw the upgrade Captain move to get out of his seat, stand up, and let the FA in while he then left the cockpit. I noticed nothing odd about his movement out of the seat and to the rear of the cockpit. I saw out of the corner of my eye the FA was standing near the rear of the cockpit just behind and to the right of the Captainâ€™s seat, a normal position for a relief FA. My concentration then focused on something else. I think it was because we were getting ready to enter a large area of convective activity. I might have been looking at WSI and comparing that to what I was seeing on the weather radar. Why my gaze was generally focused forward and right I am not sure, but it was. I planned to brief the relief FA about this weather and its possible effect on their service in a few minutes. It was at that point, maybe 30-45 seconds after the upgrade Captain had left the cockpit, that for lack of a better description, "all hell broke loose." The cockpit went from a completely benign environment to one of confusion. The startle effect was in full force. The first warning was a continuous repetitive chime and the warning lights flashing. I immediately looked at the E/WD (Engine/Warning Display) and noted about 4-5 ECAMs listed, primary secondary and independent failures in both red and amber. I silenced the CRC (Continuous Repetitive Chime) by pushing [the] master warning light. That silenced the CRC. However, there still was an aural alert going off that I could not silence, which created a fair bit of consternation on my part. I look at my PFD and saw the FMAs were wrong. I then saw the AP (Autopilot) was off and that there was nothing where I expected to see the AT (Autothrottle) condition. I noted the aircraft climbing slightly and corrected that. I knew the AP disengaged for some reason but didn't know why. I thought about engaging AP 2 but then thought that may create new problems, so I elected to hand-fly until the ECAMs were sorted out. I saw we were no longer in NAV but again, wasn't sure why. I did see that the aircraft didn't diverge much from the "green line" so lateral stick inputs weren't necessary. At this point ATC called to ask us something about recycling the transponder. We were on speaker at that time; I responded we had a problem and to standby. I then noted the airspeed increasing and pulled the TLs (Thrust Lever) back; I didn't want to add an over-speed to our problems. This silenced another aural sound. I do not recall seeing a Thrust Locked ECAM or FMA which I thought would have been the source of the alert I couldn't silence. I glanced at the Captain PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) and saw they didn't look right. The aircraft was reasonably stabilized now but, in my mind, because the ECAMs were displayed, the situation wasn't. I then told the FA to recall the trainee Captain to the cockpit. He opened the door, looked and then closed it, and said he was in the bathroom. I told the FA I knew that and I wanted him back in the cockpit now. He then had the FM knock on the Lav door. The trainee Captain returned to the cockpit and the relief FA left. The trainee Captain was incredulous when he looked at the E/WD. I told him I was hand-flying, had the aircraft and radios, and that he was to handle the ECAMs. It was at this point I noted we were about 20 knot slow, well within flying speed but slow for planned speed. I had overcompensated for my worry of overspending the aircraft. I pushed the power back up. Airspeed had fallen out of my cross-check. The trainee Captain methodically and correctly went through the ECAMs. As I recall the first several ECAMs had no action items, one ECAM had us switch the air data switch to three. At some point during this, ATC stated they now had data on us and asked if we needed assistance. We told him we were completing a procedure and to standby. Once the status messages were read and the ECAM procedure completed, I reached up to engage AP two. It did so. I armed the AT and then moved the TLs to the climb detent to engage it. Our ATC clearance was to proceed direct to a fix so we reinserted that. I don't recall having to pull or push to capture our assigned altitude but I can't be sure. It was now maybe 4-5 minutes after the initial event where I could take a breath. I recalled the ECAM and saw the ADR 1 fault. I then looked over to the ADIRS panel and saw IR mode selector one was in the OFF position. It, of course, was on for the flight up until some point in [the] last few minutes. I asked the trainee Captain if he recalls hitting the switch with his head or back as he left his seat. He said no. I then thought perhaps the switch was defective. This aircraft came to us as a through flight. We did not have to turn them on so we had no knowledge of how that switch felt by turning it on. We again discussed it and he stated he didn't recall even touching the overhead panel while leaving the seat. Because I didn't introduce myself to the FAs at the rear of the aircraft prior to the flight, I wasn't sure which FA came to the cockpit during our break. I asked the FM to ask the FA who came to the cockpit to call us on the interphone. That FA did and I asked him if he recalled touching anything on the overhead panel; he stated he did not. What I found unusual was that during the event, the FA seemed very nonplussed by the cacophony of sounds in the cockpit. I would have expected a FA to at least ask what was going on, but maybe he was somewhat shocked by what he saw and heard during his short time in the cockpit. The trainee Captain and I discussed that I would write up the ECAM and then conference Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control to provide further details of what we thought may have occurred. I wanted the switch looked at but also didn't want Maintenance to search for a problem which might not exist. I ACARSâ€™d Dispatch with the request and he set up the conference call. The communications with Technical Support Maintenance Control were reasonably good and he captured exactly what I wanted him to know and he appended it to our write-up. Since the Captainâ€™s displays were significantly degraded, we switched PF/PM roles. From that point we continually deviated for weather, were put in holding, and changed our alternate three times. We over-burned by almost 5500 lb on this flight, more than on any flight I have been on in [an] Airbus. It was an understatement to say this was a busy flight. I don't know how this happened. The final flight of the day was a termination. As the trainee ran that checklist and turned off the IRUs, he stated he couldn't believe how he accidentally managed to switch that style of switch â€“ pull and turn â€“ off by getting out of the cockpit. I am disappointed in myself for not more thoroughly reviewing the flight manual for ADR 1 fault after things had settled down. We did not have a GPWS TERR FAULT light and no ECAM direction to switch it off so it remained on. We discussed that threat in that we were now the aircraftâ€™s GPWS system and to be cognizant of the terrain. We also discussed changing the transponder to position 2 but did not do so because there was no ECAM direction to [do] so and ATC noted no anomalies in our reporting. Also, once I saw the IR mode selector switch in the off position, I should have considered reviewing the NAV IR fault non-normal even though we didn't have that ECAM. I did not do a word search in the flight manual for ADR. Had I done so, I would have seen that there may be RVSM limitations associated with its failure and should have gone to the FOM for further information. I recall many years ago, our Line Manager at the time, wrote up in his weekly update a similar event. As I recall he wrote the trainee somehow managed to hook the window shade into that same switch and turned it off. That of course didn't happen here.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported that a component was inadvertently switched off after the other pilot left the cockpit for a lavatory break and a multitude of warnings and ECAM messages went off as a result.

1.Text: On final approach, we lost the green hydraulic system. We entered holding to complete the non-normal procedure and get fully configured. We also requested a longer runway and emergency equipment. The landing was made to a full stop because of loss of normal brakes and nose wheel steering. We were then towed to the gate.

2.Text: We experienced a mechanical failure (HYD G SYS LO PRESS) upon our descent into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ1 Arrival beginning approximately outside ZZZ waypoint. I was Pilot Flying, the Captain followed appropriate ECAM actions and checklists following company procedures. We advised ATC based on this ECAM considering our location and situational aspects. We elected to hold over the final approach fix for GPS approach to Runway XX while we completed all of our necessary actions in the interest of safety. Upon completion of these duties, we exited the hold, completed approach and landed successfully coming to full stop on the runway. Based on the mechanical condition of the aircraft as result of systems lost from hydraulic system, we coordinated with company operations to tow us in due to loss of nose wheel steering and deplaned normally. Mechanical malfunction (HYD G low pressure) ECAM.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported the loss of the green hydraulic system resulted in a precautionary landing and a tow to the gate.

1.Text: After a 5 hour maintenance delay to change a flat tire, we departed for ZZZ1. We executed a normal, flex, CONF1 takeoff from [Runway] XXL in VFR weather with light winds and a light aircraft. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and was hand-flying the departure. At approximately 1,000 AGL I heard several loud bangs from the right side of the aircraft. My first thought was bird strike but the CA (Captain) called out "engine failure." I called out "my aircraft" and we determined there was a problem with the #2 engine. I don't recall any ECAMs but I do recall seeing the #2 EGT was high. I was continuing to hand-fly and CA suggested we reduce thrust to idle on the #2 engine. I agreed and we reduced the thrust and the surging and vibration ceased and the engine parameters went into the green. CA suggested an immediate return to the departure field and [advised] ATC and coordinated a downwind turn and level-off. I engaged the autopilot and prepared for a return to runway XXL with an ILS approach. CA set the FMGC up for the approach and I flew the downwind and base. CA advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) to prepare for a precautionary landing and gave a short PA as well. ATC vectored us to the ILS and cleared us for a visual approach once I had the field in sight. I executed a normal landing on XXL and we taxied clear on taxiway 1 and had the fire department inspect the aircraft. CA made several PAs instructing the passengers to remain seated and that the situation was under control. I noticed the #2 EGT was increasing and approaching the upper limit and we shut the engine down as the fire department was inspecting the engine. CA coordinated with operations a return gate and once the fire department was done and deemed the aircraft safe to taxi we returned to gate. The passengers deplaned normally. CA then called Dispatch to advise them of our return. We both determined the safest course of action was to get the aircraft back on the ground as soon as possible. This was made easier with good weather, no air traffic, and being below max. landing weight. We were only in the air ten minutes and this didn't give us time to do much troubleshooting or communication with anyone except ATC and the flight attendants. I was 100% busy flying the aircraft the entire time, but due to excellent ATC and constant communication with the Captain/PM, I felt in the yellow most of the time and in the green for the final approach and landing. I only felt I was 'in the red' for the few seconds between when the engine began surging until the CA said "engine failure." That statement immediately told me what was happening and I snapped into our trained procedures. We continued to discuss the plan and agreed that a quick return to the field was best throughout the short flight. Since the engine seemed stable at idle and we had no ECAMs we decided not to complicate things by troubleshooting but rather execute a quick precautionary landing. I feel our combined experience in the Airbus as well as constant precise communication and exchange of ideas led to the successful outcome. We backed each other up, trapped errors, and executed our plan efficiently and effectively. I don't see this event being preventable, but I think our training and emphasis on SOP and communication made for a good outcome.

2.Text: On takeoff, at approximately 1,000 feet AGL #2 engine compressor stalling with high EGT. We brought the thrust lever to idle and stalling stopped. We [notified] ATC and returned to field. Firefighters inspected the airplane and it appeared normal. Taxied to the gate.

Synopsis.Narrative: Flight Crew reported compressor stall required an air turn back and a precautionary landing.

1.Text: On climb out from ZZZ, we noticed engine oil quantity on engine #2 had gone to 0. We notified ATC and returned to ZZZ. All other indications were normal. The landing was uneventful and we taxied to the gate.

Synopsis.Narrative: First Officer reported loss of #2 engine oil quantity caused them to make an air turn back to a precautionary landing.

1.Text: On Aircraft X ZZZ1 - ZZZ during final descent I noticed an oily/burning fumes that was present in the entire AFT of the aircraft but intense towards the middle AFT of the aircraft and was coming from the air vents. We communicated with each other as a crew and confirmed that all inflight [Cabin Attendants] (F1,F2,F3,F4) detected the fumes. The intensity was a Level 2: Moderate. During this phase my symptoms were the following: burning eyes, nose and throat. Flight deck was notified. After deplaning the fumes and my symptoms dissipated. Maintenance came on board and decided we would continue our next flight with same aircraft. On Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1 during boarding when engines were turned on I immediately detected the oily burning fumes that were now at a Level 3: Strong since customers began to complain as well. The location started initially in the AFT of the aircraft but during deplaning was detectable throughout entire aircraft. The source was the same which was the air vents. The phase was during boarding on the ground. Flight deck was notified and they determined we had to deplane all customers. Myself and F4 were experiencing more severe symptoms. I experienced symptoms of burning eyes, nose and throat once again. I also began to feel tightness in my chest, difficulty breathing, thickness in the air, slight disoriented, and minor speech problems. Due to my symptoms I felt as though I was unable to perform my inflight duties safely. [Medical staff] was contacted when off the aircraft. Myself and the F4 were sent to the hospital.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Flight Attendant crew reported a fume event during boarding resulting in flight delay/cancellation.

1.Text: CA (Captain) on Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1 called and asked about NOTOC (Notice to Crew). He noticed that on walk around in ZZZ1 that human organs and dry ice was loaded on to the aircraft. ACARS was inoperative via MEL, but nowhere on the Load Closeout [documents] were restricted articles listed. I conference called the CA with CLP (Load Planning) and the CLP Supervisor said that there is nothing on their side they can do if the Crew Chief does not advise them. Also, usually a MEDEVAC notice from ATC would give us both a heads up about dry ice but they [did] not advise Dispatch. [Incomplete flight closeout documents issued due to] Missed SOP by Crew Chief. [Reporter recommends] not allow a flight closeout to be sent when a restricted item is loaded until CA acknowledges.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air Carrier Dispatch reported a communications breakdown between Dispatch and Ramp Crew Chief regarding SOP to issue required Hazmat documents.

1.Text: During the boarding process, the F/O came out of the flight deck and asked me (FA 1) to go into flight deck and to let [the flight crew] know if I smelled anything. I smelled the musty dirty sock smell. I informed the F/O that I smelled the musty odor. The Captain made an announcement to have the passengers deplane the aircraft. After all passengers deplaned, the entire flight crew went to the gate area. I called for a manager to meet us. The FA 2 complained of dizziness, FA 3 complained that her chest felt heavy. I was experiencing a bad headache initially and some minor coughing within the next hour of event. Upon driving home from the airport, approximately 2 hours from fume event; my throat became sore (difficulty with swallowing) and the cough became worse. I decided to go to Urgent Care to be assessed. They gave me a prescription with a follow up appointment for a re-check of respiratory issues.

Synopsis.Narrative: Flight Attendant reported Captain directed everyone to deplane during boarding due to a fume event.

1.Text: Previous flight had reported engine fluctuations on takeoff and climbout. Maintenance took a look at the plane and Ops checked it good. On our takeoff, once takeoff thrust was set we began a normal reduced thrust takeoff with an EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) setting of about 1.41. Once above 80 knots the Captain called out that the EGT and N1 were fluctuating and took control of the aircraft and performed the Reject. The auto brakes engaged at Max. We made the required callouts, cleared the runway and performed the QRC. We did receive HOT Brakes due to the reject and allowed them to cool before returning to the gate.

2.Text: Advancing power was normal with Flex FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) displayed and EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) thrust set prior to 80 kts. As the aircraft accelerated EPR indication on eng 1 began to fluctuate. As takoff roll continued EPR EGT and N1 began fluctuations with EPR going above yellow tick mark and almost as low as 1.3 EPR (TO EPR was 1.43). Reject was initiated at approximately 110 kts and we noticed ATC and cabin and cleared the runway to run the rejected to checklist. After allowing the brakes to cool we returned to the terminal.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported a rejected takeoff after engine fluctuations reoccurred during takeoff roll and returned to the gate.

1.Text: Aircraft was dispatched with an inoperative Pack #2 due to a regulator fault and [the flight] was in full compliance with the MEL at departure. Flight was completely full in the cabin. Due to Pack #2 being inoperative it was difficult to cool the main cabin temp using only Pack #1. Using only Pack #1 at FL370 we were able to maintain 72 degrees in the cabin using max cold and high flow. Approximately 200 nm west of ZZZ at FL370 we received an ECAM AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. ATC was notified and [priority handling was requested]. Upon checking the pressurization and bleed air page, it appeared that Pack #1 was overheating showing an output temperature in amber yet we never received a Pack 1 OVHT ECAM. The cabin altitude was still under control. A descent to 10,000 ft. was initiated without exceeding the cabin altitude before we complied with the ECAM to turn off Pack #1 leaving us unpressurized. Contact was made with Dispatch and Maintenance Control to discuss the situation resulting in a diversion to ZZZ.

2.Text: Approximately 240 nm from ZZZ, at a cruise altitude of FL350 and while in communication with Center, an ECAM aural and Master Caution sounded for AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. The CA (Captain) said he noted a momentary amber overheat temp in Pack 1, but it did not trigger the PACK 1 OVHT caution. I (Pilot Monitoring) did not see this indication that had subsequently returned to a green inlet temperature. Pack 2 was previously secured and turned off per the MEL deferral on our 2nd release. Pack 1 showed a fault light. The AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT ECAM directed us to secure Pack 1, descend to 10,000 ft. MSL or MEA and then turn on the RAM Air when the pressure differential was less than 1.0. Even though Pack 1 had a fault light in the overhead panel, it appeared to be partially functioning, the cabin pressure holding and the cabin altimeter only increasing at a very slight rate. A flight crew decision was made to begin an immediate normal descent to 10,000 ft. without the use of oxygen while closely monitoring the pressurization page to ascertain the true nature of the Pack 1 malfunction. The CA directed me to assume pilot flying duties and ATC responsibilities while he coordinated with Operations, Dispatch, flight attendants and the passengers. We began a coordinated 1500-2000 fpm rate of descent via two ATC-assigned step down altitudes of FL300 and FL200 before ultimately reaching 10,000 ft. The aircraft was lowered in a steady continual descent with no pauses which I believe helped our situation. Cabin pressure held steady around 8,000 ft. during the normal descent. Upon reaching 10,000 ft., Pack 1 was secured, differential pressure reached less than 1.0, RAM AIR was selected on and the cabin altimeter climbed from approximately 8,000 to 10,000 ft. as expected. We completed all remaining ECAM items until the screens were normal. The rate of fuel burn at 10,000 ft. MSL made reaching our initial destination of ZZZ1 impossible, and it was decided that ZZZ was a suitable diversion while 200nm away and with 11,600 pounds of fuel aboard along with the best Maintenance, aircraft and passenger accommodation options. We informed ATC, Dispatch, Operations, and proceeded accordingly. We switched to the next Center and the Captain [requested priority handling] and returned to the pilot flying role while we coordinated an uneventful arrival via the ZZZZZ to Visual XX approach at ZZZ and ultimately parking at gate XY. We were then met by the ZZZ Chief Pilot at the gate and proceeded to fill out a risk mitigation form following the event. We then accepted a new aircraft and release at gate XZ and ultimately brought the same passengers to ZZZ1 two hours later than originally planned. In totality, I felt the event was handled safely and professionally. The CRM skills taught and utilized allowed both the CA and First Officer to properly divide duties while ensuring sufficient cross checks and communication. At no time did I feel rushed or stressed. I believe the deliberate delay in securing the faulty Pack 1 that appeared to be functioning along with the continual scanning of the pressurization page allowed us to avoid an unnecessary priority descent, use of pilot oxygen, or the deployment of passenger oxygen that might have accompanied a rapid depressurization. All in all, I felt the CA was composed and handled the event in line with Company desires. While I regret the delay the passengers experienced, I believe we handled the event in a safe and caring manner.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air Carrier Pilot Crew reported departing with one air cycle machine inoperative and during cruise flight the other air cycle machine indicated a fault condition necessitating a diversion.

1.Text: Proceeding directly to ZZZZZ intersection on the ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival. Was cleared to descend via ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival on [Runway] XXR. Prior to ZZZZZ, at approximately FL220 during descent, noticed that the cabin altitude was at 8,300 feet and increasing. I called attention to the First Officer that we might be losing cabin pressurization. The Pressurization screen on ECAM was displayed and noticed that both the inlet and extract valve were fully closed but the safety valve had opened. Since we had already been cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival and had an altitude of 12,000 set in the MCP I decided to expedite the descent to see if I could control the rate of ascent in the cabin. At approximately FL180 it appeared that we could not control the rate of ascent in the cabin and that at its present rate the cabin would exceed 10,000 feet shortly. I then [advised] with ATC and requested 10,000 feet which was granted. I advised the Lead Flight Attendant that we were experiencing cabin pressurization problems but to expect a normal landing. As we leveled at 10,000 feet I monitored the cabin and noticed that it had climbed to 12,000 feet but stabilized. It took several minutes before the cabin normalized at our cruise altitude of 10,000 feet. I asked the First Officer to see if he could find an applicable checklist to run. During this time I maintained control of the aircraft and communicated with ATC. The First Officer advised that he was able to manually control the outflow valve and that the checklist recommended shallow descents thereafter. I continued to ask for delayed vectors from ATC just north of ZZZ as the First Officer and I reviewed the state of the aircraft and decided it was safe to proceed with the landing. I asked ATC for shallow descents on the arrival to [Runway] XXR into ZZZ. The landing and taxi in were uneventful.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier Captain reported malfunctioning pressurization system on descent.

1.Text: After intercepting the glideslope it was noted by both pilots the aircraft was not slowing down normally. Despite lowering the gear and deploying speedbrakes we were having a difficult time getting 10 knots below the next flap speed to continue to configure a variable tailwind was noted between 5 & 10 knots which helped explain what we were seeing. Continuing to investigate however both pilots thereafter realized we were abnormally low and the PF disconnected the AP and leveled off. Tower called with a low altitude alert shortly after that and we acknowledged it, configured normally and were stable by 500 feet AGL. Landing and roll out was normal. There were multiple approach NOTAMs that day and we miscalculated the effective times on the one stating the ILS XXL was unusable. We were an hour off and were arriving inside the last 30 minutes of the effective time. It turns out NAVAIDs maintenance was manipulating the glide slope signal at the time, causing the glide slope to appear lower. The ILS to XXL was OTS and NAVAIDs maintenance was transmitting a lower than normal glidepath. It would have been helpful if ILS status had been repeated on the ATIS, as it normally is, but it was not. During the low altitude call from tower they were even quick to add to the call that it 'was in the NOTAMs'. Further investigating with my prior position with FAA Flight Inspection it is still in their guidance that NAVAIDs maintenance is not supposed to transmit a localizer signal if they are going to manipulate the glide slope signal to avoid this hazardous, misleading, information. The localizer and glide slope both were transmitting, with a proper ID, at the time of the incident, we even crossed ZZZZZ at the appropriate altitude of 3,000 and showed on path. It was after that when the aircraft would no longer slow, as it was chasing a depressed glide path. In the end we missed the NOTAM but then multiple holes of the swiss cheese lined up; thankfully it was day VFR and we saw the solution with our own eyes in time. The other layers of protection normally there (ATIS, maintenance procedures) would have helped overcome our oversight.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported CFIT event during approach that was due to maintenance before performed on the glide slope equipment but not being announced on ATIS.

1.Text: Outbound Aircraft X on Date scheduled ZZZ-ZZZ1 had a Part Power Stops [priority package] for the flight. Our procedure is cargo goes to Operations drops off [with] paper work and Operations notifies crew chief that a Part Power Stops is scheduled for their flight. No word or mention at that time of package needing a Dangerous Goods Form. Package was loaded [in] accordance to load instruction from ZZZ1. After flight arrived in ZZZ1 and transferred to cargo. At that time it was stated a Dangerous Goods Form was required. From my understanding miscellaneous class 9 UN3373 [label] was on box. However no photos available. [Lead Avionics Technician stated] it was brought to my attention my station director [name] on DATE. Vendor in ZZZ cargo does all cargo and Part Power Stops ...they have the responsibility of knowing the contents of package and [determine] if Dangerous Goods Form is required. After being spoken to about this I did research on misc 9 UN3373 "gmmo or gmo that does not meet the definition of toxic substances or infectious substance shall be assigned a UN number. Now with that being said we do our DG training which gives us general knowledge of Hazmat material... there should be copies of all packages that originate from cargo facility so when we sign for packages we can refer to package and information to crew chief. I am not schooled enough in such practices that we can remember all package numbers that require Dangerous Goods Form. [Recommend] that all packages from cargo have to be signed for and also duplicate copies given to Ops, also oral confirmation of type package and contents.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier Inspector reported undocumented hazmat cargo was transported due to a breakdown of hazmat handling procedures.

1.Text: Just prior to leveling off at FL340, Flight Attendant called and stated there was an electrical burning smell in the forward galley. There was not any smoke nor fire, just an odor. We notified ATC, turned back toward ZZZ, accomplished all checklist items, and landed uneventfully. After clearing the runway, we had the fire department check the airplane for signs of a fire. They saw nothing so we taxied back to the gate. At the gate, the fire department came on board to check the galley. They found nothing. No deviations from FARs.

2.Text: Flight Attendant reported faint smell of fumes in forward galley. Verified by [company] deadheading pilot. Ran smoke/fumes checklist. Verified no fire or persistent fumes. Checklist said to land. Captain made the call and we returned to ZZZ. Overweight landing also accomplished and written up in ZZZ.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported an "electrical burning smell' during initial climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

1.Text: We were holding short of [the] runway and Tower reported they were seeing smoke coming from our engines but couldn't tell which one. Aircraft behind us immediately reported smoke from the #2 Engine. Tower asked us to taxi clear while I was pulling up the Engine page on the system display. I identified that the oil quantity on #2 Engine was falling rapidly from 8 quarts to 7.5 to 7 to 6.5. At that point, the aircraft behind us reported "you have flames shooting out #2". We had no flight deck indications of an engine fire during the entire event. Tower told us to stop where we were and that "we are rolling the trucks". I stopped the aircraft and called for the QRC. My FO determined we had a quick action item, ENG 1(2) FIRE (on ground). We ran the checklist which required the discharge of both fire bottles on #2 Engine. I notified the Cabin Crew, then made an announcement to the passengers and stated that we had to shut down the right engine and that we would wait for the emergency equipment to inspect the aircraft. Shortly thereafter, ARFF showed up to the aircraft while simultaneously, I was starting the APU. Upon visual inspection by ARFF, they determined there was still a small residual fire in the #2 Engine. ARFF requested that we shut down of both Engines (#2 was already properly shut down via the QRC). After the APU finished its starting cycle, I shut down the #1 Engine. As the ARFF started their fire suppression on Engine #2, I made another announcement to the passengers that they were doing this as a precaution. The First Officer and I discussed and agreed that if we needed to evacuate, it would be out the left side of the aircraft. When ARFF was finished with their visual inspection and suppression efforts, we were notified to wait for Maintenance to show up for their own inspection. When that was completed, we were told that we would be towed back to the gate. I then made another PA announcement updating the cabin crew and passengers as to what was happening. Everyone involved in this event played a significant part. Both the Tower and the aircraft behind us provided information needed to make necessary decisions due to the fact that we had no indications on the flight deck that a catastrophic engine failure was going to occur. Communication between ARFF and the flight deck was clear and concise, as was the communication with the cabin crew. By following the SOPs that are in place, a positive outcome was achieved. I'm not sure if this type of event can be prevented other than Airbus develop some kind of warning that the engine oil quantity is rapidly decreasing.

2.Text: [Report narrative contained no additional information]

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 flight crew reported Tower and another aircraft advised them of smoke coming from #2 engine during their taxi. Engine was shut down on the taxiway when the crew noted the rapidly falling oil quantity.

1.Text: As we arrived in ZZZ, the First Officer and myself had planned on the ILS to RWY (Runway) XX as the winds had favored that runway. The winds had shifted and favored RWY XY as we were handed off to approach control. As I was the flying pilot, the FO (First Officer) hastily entered the RNP to Runway XY. This was also our first time into ZZZ. As the aircraft captured Final App... it looked as if we were on profile... and we were also visual. I soon realized that the altitude constraints had not been loaded due to the fact that the approach via had not been entered. I arrested the descent, however, we did get the "pull upâ€ warning ....a go around was performed followed by the published hold. We then performed the ILS to RWY XX, circle to [Runway] XY to a normal landing.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier Flight Crew reported GPWS Alert on approach.

1.Text: Aircraft X was uneventful leading up to the approach at ZZZ. We had been cleared for the approach to Runway XX and were established on the localizer and glideslope. The autopilot and autothrust had been disengaged earlier in the approach and the aircraft had been configured to Flaps 3 when Gear Down was requested. When the gear lever was selected down the three indicators on the landing gear panel indicated red UNLK (UNLOCKED), no noise from the landing gear doors opening was heard. Captain [Name] and I communicated and confirmed on the Landing Gear Systems page that the landing gear had not extended. We decided to level out at 6,000 feet MSL while we confirmed the situation and attempted to cycle the gear. We communicated to the tower we would be going around for a landing gear failure approximately 3mi prior to the runway. Tower provided vectors and a climb to 9,000 feet, we initiated a go around over the threshold per ATC instructions and cleaned up the aircraft per SOP. The autoflight was re-engaged after the go around. During this time after the failure of subsequent attempts to cycle the gear and with the lever still down, we eventually got the L/G GEAR NOT DOWNLOCKED ECAM. The ECAM was run according to SOP by Captain [Name] while I flew the aircraft and handled radio calls. We [received priority], stated our intention to return to land on Runway XYR and requested CFR (Crash Fire Rescue Equipment). Gravity extension was successful and we were vectored to the approach. Approach and landing were normal with the exception of the gear doors remaining open. We landed with 8000 lbs. of fuel. We stopped on the runway and Operations was standing by to tow the aircraft back to the gate.

Synopsis.Narrative: First Officer reported a Go Around and precautionary landing after landing gear lock problems.

1.Text: On approach to ZZZ gear was selected down but normal gear indications did not appear and there were no associated noises such as gear extending into slipstream, etc. PF (Pilot Flying) executed a missed approach and while being vectored we tried to lower the gear normally with the same indications and we got the L/G Gear Not Down locked ECAM. Accomplishing ECAM led us to the L/G Gravity Extension QRH and after accomplishing checklist the gear safely extended. We (advised ATC) and coordinated with Flight Attendants and Dispatch and ZZZ for subsequent runway closure and tow to the gate.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported a landing gear malfunction.

1.Text: All crews should be informed and knowledgeable about emergency procedures in order to be prepared for such unexpected events in flight. After an uneventful preflight preparation and exterior inspection we departed ZZZ, myself as Pilot Flying and the Captain as Pilot Monitoring. We climbed to planned cruise altitude without issue. Shortly after reaching cruise and just south of ZZZ1, an ECAM message and associated chime presented on the lower ECAM screen indicating "ENG 1 SYSTEM FAULT". We worked through the indicated actions and referenced the COM procedures. As the engine was reduced to idle thrust only, we began a descent and began diversion planning as it became clear that we could not continue to ZZZ2 with this issue at the lower altitude required on a single engine at ZZZ3. Initially ZZZ was selected, but while I was flying and communicating with ATC the Captain in consultation with the dispatcher elected to divert instead to ZZZ4. With plenty of time to prepare we did all necessary tasks for the diversion and proceeded to an uneventful landing on ZZZ's longest runway, XXR, with fire/rescue services on standby. After landing with no issues we taxied to the assigned gate and shut down the aircraft without issue.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 First Officer reported an in-flight engine problem required a diversion and single-engine approach and landing.

1.Text: We discussed as a crew that in the future when we get pressured by time constraints and environmental pressures (i.e. raining hard during the walk around) that we won't allow ourselves to be hurried and in a rush. That is when things get missed. I missed the cowl latch key left in the Number One Engine on the preflight walk around. It was dark and raining hard and we were running a little bit late due to an excessively long line at the KCM (Known Crewmember) checkpoint.

2.Text: We discussed as a crew that in the future give us more time to get to the airplane in ZZZ with the long train ride and busy departure time. And no matter never get caught rushing any procedure. Get down on your knees and check those cowl keys! Long line at KCM (Known Crewmember) Checkpoint and we were rushing to get the flight out on time. Rainy cloudy morning in ZZZ FO (First Officer) missed cowl latch key during walk around. Proper keys and pins located on the [Aircraft] during our interior cockpit preflight. Only informed of our mistake by the outbound crew in ZZZ1. Captain called Crew Scheduling to get my number.

Synopsis.Narrative: Flight Crew reported being informed that they missed the cowling door latch key still installed in the engine cowl latch and departed.

1.Text: While working Aircraft X for a large issue with side-stay play and being the third documented discrepancy, it was requested to inspected and identify if the L/H (Left Hand) and R/H (Right Hand) side stays were still usable. It was found that they were also worn out and required replacement. Senior management refused to accept that fact and still was pressuring me for 8 hours to install the identified and documented unserviceable MLG (Main Landing Gear) side-stay assemblies and remained relentless to try any motive of pressure to have them installed with disregard with what was documented causing large amounts of stress and frustration and distraction on correctly repairing the aircraft referencing the corrected documents. Direct Supervisor and Direct Shift Manager were only relaying what was being directed and are not responsible for any pressure added. The reason for the distractions and pressure to install the side-stay assemblies that were found in poor condition for wear, was because the two side stays that were ordered could not be used until engineering had approved use and the two serviceable assemblies were the only two in the system. Senior Management was made aware that the repairs for this aircraft were going to be lengthy and to export the aircraft next door the heavy maintenance department, the discretion was ignored and they basically buried themselves into what did turn out to be a large repair on the aircraft after no side-stay assemblies were usable during the event, pressure was applied to try brush the issue out by installing the unserviceable side stays and accomplishing a visual inspection with no reference to do a visual for wear and play while installed on the aircraft. Engineering concurred the side-stay assemblies are inspected with the CMM (Component Maintenance Manual) while removed. The amount of stress and frustration with my senior management not wanting to accept the fact of what were honest documented finds after being requested to do so. The local senior management in ZZZ will not accept the reality of what large repairs are and refuse to listen and force pressure and manipulation tactics to try to get supervisors, shift managers and mechanics sign a document or stamp a block in any form possible to get what they want. It creates large safety risks and is why many of our aircraft have repeat write-ups. Senior Management relies on myself as one of the people who know how the A320F works to a detailed engineering level, until it is not the answer they want to hear. The only way to avoid the occurance would be to stop harassing people on the floor and realize that sometimes, it is what it is after poor managerial decisions were made.

Synopsis.Narrative: Technician reported resisting pressure from management to install unserviceable side stays during a MLG strut change and refused the work.

1.Text: Ops normal from pushback to takeoff roll. I was flying pilot, [the] Captain non-flying pilot. Power was set and autothrottles and FMAs all had normal indications. At approximately 60 knots there was a loud bang and the jet swerved to the right. I steered the jet back to centerline with rudder and the Captain initiated the abort. We stopped quickly on the runway and told ATC we'd aborted and instructed the passengers to remain seated. After quickly assessing the risk, and talking with the Lead Flight Attendant, Captain determined it was safe to taxi clear of Runway XX and we stopped on the parallel taxiway. We requested assistance from [the] Fire Department to look at the landing gear to ensure we hadn't blown a tire or had smoke/fire coming off the brakes. After getting the all-clear, we coordinated with Operations/Tech Ops to return to Gate X. We closely monitored brake temp indications during the taxi back and saw that they were all decreasing in normal fashion as expected. We were met by many company personnel at the gate and Maintenance was able to quickly determine we had an Engine Number 2 compressor stall during takeoff roll. Passengers deplaned in normal fashion through Door 1L, and the flight crew was then escorted up to ZZZ Flight Ops to discuss our readiness and ability to continue flying the trip. Captain and I then proceeded to fly as scheduled.

2.Text: During takeoff roll, heard a loud bang and aircraft swerved to the right. Executed rejected takeoff procedure. Exited runway. Personnel inspected aircraft externally. No visible damage and no fires were detected. Returned to gate. Maintenance data showed engine stall on Number 2 Engine. My compliments to the First Officer and Flight Attendants for their professionalism during this unexpected event.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier flight crew reported that an engine compressor stall occurred during takeoff roll, causing the aircraft to swerve and the crew to reject the takeoff.

1.Text: Aircraft X in ZZZ with pilot discrepancy "F/CTL FLAPS FAULT. ECAM OCCURRED ON APPROACH WHEN MOVING FLAP LEVER FROM 1 TO 2. AFTER RECYCLING FLAP LEVER PER ECAM, FLAPS OPERATED NORMALLY." Post flight report indicated flap jam in flight phase 6 cruise. 4th shift started troubleshooting per TSM and I was assigned to continue. TSM stated both flap actuators were required to be changed in the event of a jam with no faults due to known icing problem. Concurred with Maintenance Control that this was desired and safest step to continue. Gave all information to my crew chief, and supervisor and that the plane needs to be taken out of service until the parts are removed and replaced. Supervisor outlined that his boss argued that it's not the problem and proceeded to find any way to keep aircraft green. Both myself and work partner were pressured for well over the night to not ground Aircraft X and call it good. We raised the fact the TSM explicitly states with no faults both actuators must be changed. Due to ongoing peer pressure I reluctantly agreed to sign Aircraft X airworthy on the technicality that although the aircraft is reporting a flap jam, the phase of flight it occurred was in cruise and probably an indication error. However, prior to Date on Date-1 the exact fault and exact write up was entered. Corrective action from ZZZ2 base was a reset of LH #1 torque limiter. The TSM for this faults states that when resetting a flap torque limiter, the TSM refers to lubricate drive system, do a detail inspection and replace rotary actuator which have a tripped torque limiter. This was not done in ZZZ2 when an indicator was tripped, reset, and signed off. See [Logbook Entry]. I advised Maintenance Control and supervision of this oversight and advocated for replacing flap actuators. Event occurred because management doesn't take un airworthy as acceptable. Keep management where it belongs. Managing their supervisors and leave the technical aspect to the mechanics with the proper steps and actions from the manuals.

2.Text: Plane arrived in ZZZ with Flight CTL flap slat fault, was written up previous day for same thing. Contract maintenance with Maintenance Control guidance troubleshot fault - no faults where found, we ran engines and cycled the flaps per Maintenance Control request, no faults occurred. Approaching ZZZ1 at 2,000 ft. at flaps 2 selected we had a ECAM FLT CTL FLAPS FAULT message. Did go around and followed vectors to 3,000 ft., advised ATC and followed QRH, We did all steps but were both misinterpreted the checklist. Should have put lever to flaps 3, instead of flaps full and calculated the wrong approach speed as we now believe we misinterpreted the max speed chart for approach speed. 190 kts. instead of 165 kts. Report said we were 185 kts. I believe. On the approach I knew something was not right, thought about going around but was worried about the fuel time. During approach we had full slats no flaps. We requested longer runway (12,000 ft.), Landing was normal I let plane slow to 100 kts. before applying breaks. Never heated up beyond 150 [degrees] more or less. After firefighters looked over the airplane we proceeded to gate. Should have referred to SOP in performance for added info but thought we were right and worried about fuel. I have done this procedure in training, I ran the checklist and made the mistake that I was warned about. I believe frustration with a reassignment, irritated with a broken airplane (multiple problems) that was delivered to us and worried about fuel during checklist all added to my distraction and lead me to misinterpreting the checklist. Slow down slow read checklist slower, have more fuel to run all the way through.

Synopsis.Narrative: Multiple repeat flap failures caused a no flap landing and subsequent errors during maintenance trouble shooting and repair of the affected system.

1.Text: Additional safety concerns regarding refusal to operate Aircraft X: The deferral of Slat Flap Controller Computer (SFCC) #2 and SFCC Chanel #2 Results in degraded functionality of slats and flaps, (Slow operation). SFCC1 and related protections from Wing Tip Brakes (WTBS) is only remaining operative system with no redundancy. We also have another flight control related deferral with an inoperative rudder travel limiter. Any other flight control computer(s) becoming inoperative during flight would further degrade your ability to control the aircraft i.e., Elevator and Aileron Computers (ELACs), Secondary Computers (SECs), Flight Augmentation Computers (FACs) etc. all of which must be operational for dispatch due to the seriousness of the deferral. Both my First Officer and I were in agreement with the unacceptably reduced safety margins of this aircraft. Please include the above safety concerns with my originally filed report. I was very tired after a long day, and didn't have time to write a full and proper report which I intended to do.

Synopsis.Narrative: Air carrier Captain refused an aircraft due to a deferred Slat Flap Controller Computer, citing concerns that flight control protections would be reduced if other computers were to fail in flight.

1.Text: We were dispatched with an inoperative SFCC#2 (Slat Flap Control Computer) and Inoperative SFCC#2 Channel. This deferral negatively affected the safety of flight. Operating an electric airplane with inoperative flight control computers is not safe. I called Dispatch and Maintenance Control in order to make the proper refusal.

Synopsis.Narrative: A320 Captain reported concerns with being dispatched with an inoperative Slat Flap Control Computer.

1.Text: I was the Captain on Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Date.
